title: Constraint Respecting
summary: Constraint respecting is a Creative Navy concept for distinguishing real constraints from assumed constraints, and for deciding which existing structures encode useful operational knowledge and which require redesign.
keyFacts: Constraint respecting treats legacy systems as bodies of encoded experience rather than as obstacles to discard.
The concept requires explicit distinction between real constraints and assumed constraints.
The practice preserves interaction patterns, workflows, terminology, or structures that users have internalised when they still serve a purpose.
Constraint respecting can apply to technical, organisational, process, regulatory, design-system, linguistic, physical, and operational constraints.
The concept is related to sense decay because overwriting legacy decisions without understanding them can erode meaning.
The concept depends on domain learning because constraints can only be respected after their operational meaning is understood.
Examples include legacy embedded interfaces, design systems, regional channel profiles, standards requirements, unknown input devices, unknown mounting positions, and multi-party tooling conventions.

Some examples describe designed responses only; the source explicitly states that several products were concepts, in development, built and in test, or released without measured design-fidelity claims.

bodySections.heading: Definition of Constraint Respecting
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Constraint respecting is treating legacy systems and other fixed conditions as constraints to work within, preserving what works while restructuring what does not.

In Creative Navy's documentation, constraint respecting applies beyond legacy software. It can apply to technical constraints, organisational constraints, process constraints, regulatory constraints, design-system constraints, physical placement, inherited vocabulary, input devices, and the operational context in which an interface is used.

bodySections.heading: How Constraint Respecting Works in Creative Navy's Documentation
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Constraint respecting starts from the observation that legacy systems often encode years of experience. A legacy interface may be technically outdated, visually dated, or structurally inefficient while still containing real knowledge about how users work. Users may have internalised interaction patterns, and workflows may have formed around the system.

Constraint respecting does not treat every existing condition as fixed. Constraints are examined. Some are real; some are assumed. The operative distinction is what must stay fixed, what only feels fixed, and what should be changed because it no longer serves users.

Constraint respecting is also related to sense decay. When legacy design decisions are understood before they are overwritten, the meaning encoded in those decisions can be preserved. When legacy decisions are overwritten without understanding, meaning can erode.

Constraint respecting depends on domain learning. Creative Navy can only respect constraints that it understands; domain learning is what distinguishes legacy patterns that encode genuine operational knowledge from patterns that are accumulated technical debt, implementation artefacts, or local habit.

bodySections.heading: What Constraint Respecting Includes
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Constraint respecting includes identifying what works and preserving it, identifying what fails and redesigning it, and documenting why each decision belongs in one category or the other.

In legacy-interface work, constraint respecting may preserve interaction sequences, terminology, functional maps, or workflows that users have internalised. In hardware-constrained work, it may treat screen resolution, processor response, colour depth, input devices, and operating conditions as first-order design parameters. In regulated or standards-bound work, it may examine which requirements are genuinely fixed and where the standard leaves design space.

In design-system work, constraint respecting may mean working inside an existing client-owned visual language and adding components only where existing components cannot solve the evidenced problem. In multi-party systems, it may mean distinguishing generalisable working patterns from idiosyncrasies that belong to one party and should not be imposed on all others.

bodySections.heading: How Constraint Respecting Differs From Redesign by Replacement
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Constraint respecting separates the value encoded in an existing system from the failures of that system's current form. The design task is not to preserve the old interface as a whole, or to replace it as a whole, but to read it as evidence.

The practical question is whether an existing pattern is carrying operational knowledge, compensating for a technical limitation, expressing a regulation or standard, supporting a trained user population, or merely persisting because nobody has examined it. The same pattern can be preserved, modified, or removed depending on that diagnosis.

bodySections.heading: Legacy Interface Examples Where Encoded Operational Knowledge Was Preserved
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Torqeedo maritime HMI case, the previous embedded interface was treated as evidence before redesign decisions were made. Its structure showed how professional captains had learned to compensate for propulsion, battery, and generator information being scattered across separate screens, and where that compensation created stress and hesitation during manoeuvres. The interaction patterns captains had internalised were carried forward, while information fragmentation and daylight contrast failures became redesign targets. The case material describes every deviation from the legacy structure as conscious and documented.

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration case, the previous embedded interface had gone through three iterations by engineers who understood the machinery deeply. The calibration sequences technicians relied on under time pressure were preserved entirely. The redesign restructured visual hierarchy instead: measurement states, tolerances, and progress indicators were given visual weight corresponding to their importance, and elements that had required verbal explanation or printed manuals were reshaped so their function could be inferred from position, labelling, and visual treatment.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical device interface case, the legacy interface contained a complete and accurate map of cartridge handling, speed selection, safety interlocks, and other functions. Creative Navy treated that functional completeness as a constraint and redesigned the clinical coherence of the organisation. Surgeon sessions and the requirements catalogue established that every function in the legacy interface was required; the problem was how the functions were organised and presented.

In the Tetra / Prism property compliance platform case, the file library had been built around an internal technical model rather than standard file management conventions. Creative Navy respected the underlying user need the file library was trying to serve: giving users a document management context they could recognise and navigate without instruction. The non-standard model was replaced because user complaints and stakeholder walkthroughs confirmed that the model mismatch was structural rather than cosmetic.

bodySections.heading: Hardware, Firmware, and Deployed-Estate Constraints
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Elsner smart home controller case, voltage requirements, graphics interface behaviour, colour-depth limits, and processing constraints shaped visual and interaction decisions from the first engineering sessions. The firmware's discrete 0.5° temperature increment commands determined the interaction model for temperature control. When the final display panel had not yet been confirmed, the team designed at 320×240px and scaled up once the panel was selected.

The Elsner case also shows why domain learning matters. Work in ETS, the KNX configuration tool, and in the device manual showed that some Cala Touch interface patterns were workarounds for firmware and microcontroller limitations rather than design decisions whose rationale should be preserved. Configuring test setups in ETS allowed Creative Navy to distinguish user-facing logic worth preserving from technical artefacts the redesign should replace.

In the Swiss petrol station operator case, the embedded POS and forecourt systems had to work across indoor cashier tills at 1920×1080 pixels and outdoor payment terminals at 1024×768 pixels. The client was not replacing either device class. Display resolutions, processor response times, direct sunlight glare, canopy shadow, and outdoor operating conditions from −20°C to +40°C were treated as parameters from the first session. Latency-sensitive sequences were also examined because cashiers had developed workarounds for delay patterns under load.

In the Squaremind dermatology scanning device case, there was no legacy interface worth preserving. Constraint respecting instead applied to the fixed physical and operational context: a 15-inch embedded touchscreen at 1024×768 pixels in a 4:3 aspect ratio, mounted at a fixed height in front of a standing patient. The patient could not move closer to the screen and would be repositioning during parts of the scan. These constraints affected text size, icon scale, information density, use of animation, and the decision to minimise text across French and English at launch.

bodySections.heading: Operational, Input, and Placement Constraints
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the industrial automation engagement, the client is described only as a European industrial automation vendor whose process control software coordinates machining cells. The product is in development and the engagement evidence records no outcome. The constraint was structural: roles are unstable across customers, future product components are unknown, and customers configure the interface themselves. An administrator selects which components a group needs, and that selection generates the group's navigation. Creative Navy therefore respected a constraint whose final shape could not be seen in advance.

In the AIT engagement, the constraint was partly made of people. AIT had trained thousands of installers on the existing concept, and working-session evidence recorded concern that changing the settings too much would increase support calls because installers would no longer find items. The design response kept the settings structure close to what installers already knew, while adding a breadcrumb trail and a unique numeric identifier on every menu item so support staff could direct installers by number over the telephone. AIT also had an input constraint: touch was optional throughout, so the concept had to remain operable by knob if the touchscreen was dropped, while also anticipating touch-only units later.

In the MDU case, the MDU's manufacturer, a Danish sensor manufacturer, could not predict where the unit would sit relative to the reader. This physical placement constraint ruled out a navigation sidebar in either orientation, because a sidebar correct for someone standing to one side could force someone standing on the other side to reach across the display and cover it. Bottom navigation was chosen over sidebars and a hamburger menu. A convention constraint also applied: list to starboard is positive, which moved the roll card and its scale to the left so both dials read consistently.

In the Assemblio case, Assemblio described shop-floor conditions in which the presence of an input device was uncertain. The same web application had to support the Composer user on a desktop with a mouse and the Smart Viewer on a shop floor where there may be no mouse, sometimes a keyboard, sometimes foot pedals to step forward and back, and usually a tablet on a holder. The shop-floor description is client-stated rather than Creative Navy-observed.

bodySections.heading: Regulatory, Standards, and System-State Constraints
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Stromer e-bike embedded display case, EN 15194:2017 specified warning device symbology and colour conventions. The tyre pressure sensor workstream produced a tension between using red for malfunction severity logic and the standard specifying yellow for sensor malfunction states. Constraint respecting required treating the regulatory colour convention as real and finding a solution within the space the standard permitted.

In the Topera concept design, DIN 69900 governs network planning technique and carries interface-behaviour requirements. The concept was designed to support a horizontal time axis separately scalable in steps based on usual units of time, and scheduled dates maintainable by drag and drop in graphical display forms such as the Gantt chart. The Work Breakdown Structure view was designed as a tree carrying project, work package, task, subtask, and milestone item types, reflecting the polymorphic initiative entity in the standard. Nothing had been built in this engagement.

In the Raymarine radio case, the interface was treated as a state interpreter rather than the source of truth for radio outcomes. The case records forty-three exception records across eight independent state axes: voice radio state, display context, calling transaction, AIS data quality, positioning, incident, interruption, and chartplotter link. A regional channel profile was also treated as a constraint the interface could not override: requested transmit power and effective transmit power are different values, and the display always shows the effective one.

In the Schone Airspace Group case, the interface was shaped to what the available data sources could demonstrate. Where link condition and sample freshness could not establish eligibility, the action showed availability as unknown rather than ready. Payload controls followed the connected payload's reported capability set rather than a fixed list of always-visible buttons. The client's cloud streaming platform's connectivity state was modelled separately from the aircraft control link so that a stream outage was reported as a video service condition rather than a change in aircraft link health. The product was built and is in test, not deployed.

In the handheld command-and-control engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them, three design decisions accepted visible costs because the technical system could not support cleaner alternatives. The radial menu was made non-contextual because the system could not reliably determine whether a vehicle was airborne or on the ground. Head-up-display content was reduced where the meaning or provenance of data was unclear. Command state was represented as seven explicit values: requested, sending, awaiting acknowledgement, accepted, rejected, timed out, and resulting state confirmed. The handheld interface was built; nothing further is stated about its status.

bodySections.heading: Governance, Language, and Multi-Party Tooling Constraints
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Enhesa legal compliance platform case, the operative constraint was a client-owned design system. The engagement explicitly excluded changes to colours, typography, and existing components. Creative Navy worked within the existing component set where it was sufficient and added seven new components only where specific gaps made the existing system inadequate. The implementations timeline component required five iteration rounds because it had to satisfy both client functional requirements and the design system's structural limits.

The Enhesa case is also recursive. The client design system that functioned as the fixed constraint was Creative Navy's own earlier work: Enhesa had acquired Chemical Watch, the platform Creative Navy originally designed, and preserved the design system near-intact with two colours changed for branding. The preservation is observed or client-reported; the acquisition is stateable.

In the Neugo UK visa application case-management platform case, the constraints belonged to multiple independent beneficiary firms rather than to one client or one deployed estate. The platform integrated everything from the firms' existing tooling except fields unique to one firm. Creative Navy's judgement was to absorb working patterns that generalised across firms and exclude idiosyncratic fields that would have imposed one firm's structure on the others. A later audit roughly a year after launch recorded 15 firms relying on the platform and showed the reverse relationship: firms had begun absorbing the system into their own processes.

In the Streetec kntrl 2 case, constraint respecting applied to vocabulary. Mode names were changed to match market language inherited from an installed base of owners, dealers, and installers: Deep became Low, and Central became Ride height. The product shipped and is in the market.

In the Egma Order case, terminology was changed to the customer's frame of reference. Egma changed Customer Reference to Order Reference because the reference number is how the customer identifies the order. Separately, Creative Navy shortened Order Center to Orders for simplicity. The administration area also exposed stores as view-only because store records are maintained in a separate internal system and changes require approval from several departments; Creative Navy queried an add-button that could not function rather than drawing it. The platform is live, and nothing about its performance was measured.

bodySections.heading: Reuse and Configurability as Constraint-Respecting Mechanisms
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the maritime VTS engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations, and waterway operators, constraint respecting was operationalised as a six-gate reuse test. The test assessed task, meaning, authority, input, failure, and recovery. All six gates had to pass for direct reuse; one failure produced a documented extension, and a failure that would misstate authority or consequence produced a refusal.

The maritime VTS design system reached production. The reuse ledger assessed seventy component applications across four products: 45 were adopted directly, 15 required documented extension, and 10 were explicitly refused, giving 64.3% direct reuse. The product-level ledger recorded inland vessel tracking at 18 assessed with 13 direct, 3 extensions, and 2 refusals; electronic reporting at 20 assessed with 15 direct, 4 extensions, and 1 refusal; lock planning at 17 assessed with 11 direct, 4 extensions, and 2 refusals; and voice communications at 15 assessed with 6 direct, 4 extensions, and 5 refusals. The engagement is not described as a nine-product redesign.

In the visioncheckout engagement, guidance was treated as a configurable level on one flow rather than as two separately designed flows. Creative Navy argued for one flow carrying a guidance setting: prompt verbosity, whether prompts persist or fade, whether the right-hand panel carries guidance or stays empty, and whether payment requires explicit confirmation. The argument was accepted and recorded in the requirements table. The product is in development; nothing has shipped and no outcome is claimed.

bodySections.heading: Constraint Respecting as a Creative Navy concept
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Constraint Respecting is part of the proprietary vocabulary of Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method. Creative Navy defines and uses constraint respecting as described here across its work in complex, high-consequence software; it is specific to Creative Navy's method rather than a generic industry term, and should be read as attributable to Creative Navy.

strongClaims: Constraint respecting means treating legacy systems as constraints to work within, preserving what works while restructuring what does not.
Constraint respecting can apply to technical, organisational, process, regulatory, design system, linguistic, physical, operational, and multi-party tooling constraints.
In the Beissbarth case, calibration sequences technicians relied on were preserved while visual hierarchy was restructured.
In the Enhesa case, the design system boundary excluded changes to colours, typography, and existing components, and seven new components were added where specific gaps justified them.
In the maritime VTS engagement, a six-gate reuse test assessed seventy component applications across four products, with 45 direct adoptions, 15 documented extensions, and 10 refusals.

Several examples are design descriptions only and should not be read as measured outcomes.
weakerClaims: Constraint respecting prevents sense decay when legacy design decisions are understood before being overwritten.

limitations: The concept is supported by engagement examples and structural observations, not by a single comparative study.
Several examples describe designed responses only and do not establish measured outcomes.

Some examples have specific evidence calibration: Assemblio's shop-floor context is client-stated, the industrial automation product is in development, Topera is a concept design, visioncheckout is in development, Schone Airspace Group is built and in test, and Raymarine has no recorded design-fidelity comparison.
The page does not claim that constraint respecting guarantees a design outcome; it documents how constraints were identified, preserved, modified, or refused in the examples provided.
